plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 22: Electric Charges and Fields
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic three-dimensional depiction of a hydrogen atom drawn as one large sphere. The sphere is rendered as a grey outline circle with a paler grey ellipse across its middle standing for an equatorial plane, which gives the drawing depth. At the center sits a small dark blue disc bearing a plus sign, representing the proton. A second, much smaller pale blue sphere representing the electron is placed on the upper right of the spherical surface, and a thin blue arc curves down to it from the top of the sphere. A straight black line labeled r joins the central charge to the electron, and a thick red arrow labeled F lies along that same line, pointing from the electron back toward the nucleus. A vertical dashed line through the center, a horizontal dashed line across the equatorial ellipse, and faint blue dashed guides dropping from the electron to that ellipse fix the electron's position in three dimensions. Drawing the force antiparallel to r conveys at a glance that the interaction is attractive and directed along the line joining the two particles. The sketch sets up a Coulomb's law calculation of the force on the ground-state electron at its most probable distance from the proton.

elements: large outline sphere (grey great-circle silhouette) representing the hydrogen atom / electron's spherical shell
pale grey equatorial ellipse across the middle of the sphere (equatorial plane seen edge-on-ish)
small dark-blue disc with a white '+' sign at the sphere's center — the proton (nucleus)
small pale-blue sphere on the upper-right of the spherical surface — the electron
thin blue meridian arc curving from the top (north pole) of the sphere down to the electron
straight black line segment from proton to electron, labeled 'r'
thick red arrow lying along that same line, tail at the electron, head pointing back toward the proton, labeled 'F'
vertical black dashed line through the sphere center (polar axis), extending above and below the sphere
horizontal black dashed line across the equatorial ellipse through the center
faint blue dashed vertical drop line from the electron down to the equatorial plane
faint blue dashed radial line in the equatorial plane from the center out to the foot of that drop line
italic text labels 'r' (above the segment) and 'F' (below/right of the red arrow)

interactions.teaches: The Coulomb force is a central force: wherever the electron sits on the shell, r and F stay along the same line and F always points back at the proton — the interaction is attractive and radial, independent of direction.

interactions.label: Separation r (Bohr radii, a₀ = 5.29×10⁻¹¹ m)
interactions.teaches: Force magnitude obeys the inverse square law — halving r quadruples the arrow length while its direction stays exactly radial.
The electron really is off the equatorial plane in depth; rotating shows the dashed guides are a 3D coordinate drop, not a flat triangle.

demo_steps.title: Ground state, as drawn
demo_steps.narration: The proton sits at the center of the sphere and the electron rides on the shell at the most probable distance, one Bohr radius away. The black segment r and the red arrow F lie along the same line, but F points inward.

demo_steps.title: Move the electron around the shell
demo_steps.narration: Drag the electron anywhere on the sphere. The meridian arc, the dashed drop lines, r and F all follow — F never stops pointing at the proton, because the Coulomb force is central.

demo_steps.title: Pull the electron farther out
demo_steps.narration: At r = 2a₀ the direction of F is unchanged but the arrow shrinks to one quarter of its length: F = ke²/r².

demo_steps.title: Squeeze it closer
demo_steps.narration: At r = 0.5a₀ the arrow grows four times longer — the attraction climbs steeply as the electron approaches the nucleus.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: outer sphere radius R = 2.0 units, centered at the origin; this R corresponds to one Bohr radius a₀ = 5.29×10⁻¹¹ m at the slider default of 1.0 (so slider value s places the electron at radius 2.0·s units, and the sphere itself should rescale with s so the electron always rides ON the drawn shell). Sphere drawn as a translucent/wireframe silhouette only: grey great-circle outline #B0B0B0, ~2 px. Equatorial ellipse lies in the y = 0 plane (the XZ plane), drawn pale grey #CFCFCF; from the standard axonometric pose it reads as a wide flat ellipse about 4.0 units wide and ~0.8 units tall on screen, i.e. viewed from roughly 12–15° above the plane — the camera is only slightly above the equator. Proton: dark navy disc #16466E with a thin lighter blue ring and a white '+' glyph, radius ~0.16 units, at the origin. Electron: pale steel-blue sphere #7FB3D5 with slightly darker outline, radius ~0.10 units, positioned upper-right at azimuth ≈ 35° toward the viewer's right-front and elevation ≈ 42° above the equatorial plane (screen position: right of the vertical dashed axis, roughly two-thirds of the way up the sphere). Meridian arc: medium blue #2E86AB, ~1.5 px, running along the sphere surface from the north pole (0, +R, 0) down the electron's own meridian to the electron — it curves down and to the right. Segment r: solid black ~1.5 px from proton to electron; label 'r' in italic serif placed just above-left of the segment's upper half. Force arrow F: thick dark red #A92E22 (~5 px shaft with a broad filled arrowhead) starting at the electron and ending short of the proton, pointing exactly antiparallel to r; label 'F' in italic serif just below-right of the arrow's midpoint. Vertical dashed line: black, dash ~0.12/0.10, along +Y and −Y through the center, extending ~0.6 units beyond the sphere top and reaching the bottom of the sphere. Horizontal dashed line: black, along the screen-horizontal diameter of the equatorial ellipse, extending slightly past the ellipse on both sides. Guide lines from the electron: light blue #9FC8E0 dashed — one vertical drop from the electron straight down (−Y) to its foot point on the equatorial plane, and one from that foot point back to the center along the plane. Coulomb value for correctness: F = k e²/r² with k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C², e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C; at r = a₀ = 5.29×10⁻¹¹ m this gives F ≈ 8.25×10⁻⁸ N. Draw the arrow length proportional to 1/s² with the default (s = 1) length ≈ 0.55·R, clamped to ≤ 0.9·R so it never overshoots the proton.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the sphere silhouette with a THREE.LineLoop great circle that is re-oriented each frame to face the camera (or a MeshBasicMaterial sphere with very low opacity plus an EdgesGeometry-free outline ring) so it always reads as a clean circle during orbit. Equatorial ellipse = flat circle of radius R in the XZ plane drawn as a line loop. Dashed lines need LineDashedMaterial with computeLineDistances(). The red F arrow is best as a custom mesh (CylinderGeometry shaft + ConeGeometry head) grouped and oriented with quaternion setFromUnitVectors so it can rescale in length without distorting the head. Labels 'r' and 'F' as CSS2DRenderer/sprite labels anchored to the segment midpoint and offset a few pixels so they never overlap the arrow. Drag: raycast the pointer against an invisible sphere of radius R and snap the electron to the hit point; suppress OrbitControls while the pointer is down on the electron (set controls.enabled = false on pointerdown over the electron). Recompute the meridian arc as a QuadraticBezier/spherical interpolation between the north pole and the electron each drag frame. Slider should scale the whole shell, the electron radius position, the guide lines and the arrow together in one update function. Render order: dashed guides first, then sphere outline, then r segment, then arrow, then charges on top with depthTest disabled for the proton/electron discs so they stay visible through the shell.

authoredContext:
The Force on the Electron in Hydrogen A hydrogen atom consists of a single proton and a single electron. The proton has a charge of +e and the electron has −e. In the “ground state” of the atom, the electron orbits the proton at most probable distance of 5.29×10−11m (the figure). Calculate the electric force on the electron due to the proton.

A schematic depiction of a hydrogen atom, showing the force on the electron. This depiction is only to enable us to calculate the force; the hydrogen atom does not really look like this. Recall another section.

A positive charge is shown at the center of a sphere of radius r. An electron is depicted as a particle on the sphere. The force on the electron is along the radius, toward the nucleus.

Strategy For the purposes of this example, we are treating the electron and proton as two point particles, each with an electric charge, and we are told the distance between them; we are asked to calculate the force on the electron. We thus use Coulomb’s law.

Coulomb force on the H-atom electron
Drag the pale-blue electron to slide it anywhere on the shell — r and F stay on one line. Drag the white background to orbit the figure; scroll to zoom.

discrepancies: In the source the dashed polar axis runs the full height of the figure (well above the sphere and through the proton); the generated version stops just above the shell, and the dashed equatorial line is similarly shortened.

The red F arrow in the source spans roughly half the radius with a prominent head starting right at the electron; the generated arrow is comparatively short/thin, weakening the visual pairing with the black r segment.
Generated figure adds elements not in the source: a faint blue translucent shell fill and a 'proton (+)' text label under the nucleus.

The shell radius is scaled as r^0.35 rather than proportionally to r, so moving the separation slider to 2a₀ barely enlarges the sphere — the geometric meaning of r is visually understated even though the numeric readout doubles.
The in-panel slider caption 'Separation r = 1.00 a₀' wraps into a one-character-per-line vertical stack, making the primary control hard to read.
evaluation.notes: A close, well-composed reproduction of the Bohr-atom Coulomb-force figure with correct primitives, colors and rich, pedagogically meaningful interactions; weaknesses are a compressed (non-proportional) shell-radius scaling with r, a shorter-than-source force arrow, truncated dashed axes, and a badly wrapping slider caption.

feedback.rationale: The concept and primitives are correct; remaining issues are concrete implementation details (proportional shell scaling, arrow length, dashed axis extents, extra elements, wrapping slider caption) that belong to the generator.

plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 22: Electric Charges and Fields
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic three-dimensional depiction of a hydrogen atom drawn as one large sphere. The sphere is rendered as a grey outline circle with a paler grey ellipse across its middle standing for an equatorial plane, which gives the drawing depth. At the center sits a small dark blue disc bearing a plus sign, representing the proton. A second, much smaller pale blue sphere representing the electron is placed on the upper right of the spherical surface, and a thin blue arc curves down to it from the top of the sphere. A straight black line labeled r joins the central charge to the electron, and a thick red arrow labeled F lies along that same line, pointing from the electron back toward the nucleus. A vertical dashed line through the center, a horizontal dashed line across the equatorial ellipse, and faint blue dashed guides dropping from the electron to that ellipse fix the electron's position in three dimensions. Drawing the force antiparallel to r conveys at a glance that the interaction is attractive and directed along the line joining the two particles. The sketch sets up a Coulomb's law calculation of the force on the ground-state electron at its most probable distance from the proton.

elements: large outline sphere (grey great-circle silhouette) representing the hydrogen atom / electron's spherical shell
pale grey equatorial ellipse across the middle of the sphere (equatorial plane seen edge-on-ish)
small dark-blue disc with a white '+' sign at the sphere's center — the proton (nucleus)
small pale-blue sphere on the upper-right of the spherical surface — the electron
thin blue meridian arc curving from the top (north pole) of the sphere down to the electron
straight black line segment from proton to electron, labeled 'r'
thick red arrow lying along that same line, tail at the electron, head pointing back toward the proton, labeled 'F'
vertical black dashed line through the sphere center (polar axis), extending above and below the sphere
horizontal black dashed line across the equatorial ellipse through the center
faint blue dashed vertical drop line from the electron down to the equatorial plane
faint blue dashed radial line in the equatorial plane from the center out to the foot of that drop line
italic text labels 'r' (above the segment) and 'F' (below/right of the red arrow)

interactions.teaches: The Coulomb force is a central force: wherever the electron sits on the shell, r and F stay along the same line and F always points back at the proton — the interaction is attractive and radial, independent of direction.

interactions.label: Separation r (Bohr radii, a₀ = 5.29×10⁻¹¹ m)
interactions.teaches: Force magnitude obeys the inverse square law — halving r quadruples the arrow length while its direction stays exactly radial.
The electron really is off the equatorial plane in depth; rotating shows the dashed guides are a 3D coordinate drop, not a flat triangle.

demo_steps.title: Ground state, as drawn
demo_steps.narration: The proton sits at the center of the sphere and the electron rides on the shell at the most probable distance, one Bohr radius away. The black segment r and the red arrow F lie along the same line, but F points inward.

demo_steps.title: Move the electron around the shell
demo_steps.narration: Drag the electron anywhere on the sphere. The meridian arc, the dashed drop lines, r and F all follow — F never stops pointing at the proton, because the Coulomb force is central.

demo_steps.title: Pull the electron farther out
demo_steps.narration: At r = 2a₀ the direction of F is unchanged but the arrow shrinks to one quarter of its length: F = ke²/r².

demo_steps.title: Squeeze it closer
demo_steps.narration: At r = 0.5a₀ the arrow grows four times longer — the attraction climbs steeply as the electron approaches the nucleus.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: outer sphere radius R = 2.0 units, centered at the origin; this R corresponds to one Bohr radius a₀ = 5.29×10⁻¹¹ m at the slider default of 1.0 (so slider value s places the electron at radius 2.0·s units, and the sphere itself should rescale with s so the electron always rides ON the drawn shell). Sphere drawn as a translucent/wireframe silhouette only: grey great-circle outline #B0B0B0, ~2 px. Equatorial ellipse lies in the y = 0 plane (the XZ plane), drawn pale grey #CFCFCF; from the standard axonometric pose it reads as a wide flat ellipse about 4.0 units wide and ~0.8 units tall on screen, i.e. viewed from roughly 12–15° above the plane — the camera is only slightly above the equator. Proton: dark navy disc #16466E with a thin lighter blue ring and a white '+' glyph, radius ~0.16 units, at the origin. Electron: pale steel-blue sphere #7FB3D5 with slightly darker outline, radius ~0.10 units, positioned upper-right at azimuth ≈ 35° toward the viewer's right-front and elevation ≈ 42° above the equatorial plane (screen position: right of the vertical dashed axis, roughly two-thirds of the way up the sphere). Meridian arc: medium blue #2E86AB, ~1.5 px, running along the sphere surface from the north pole (0, +R, 0) down the electron's own meridian to the electron — it curves down and to the right. Segment r: solid black ~1.5 px from proton to electron; label 'r' in italic serif placed just above-left of the segment's upper half. Force arrow F: thick dark red #A92E22 (~5 px shaft with a broad filled arrowhead) starting at the electron and ending short of the proton, pointing exactly antiparallel to r; label 'F' in italic serif just below-right of the arrow's midpoint. Vertical dashed line: black, dash ~0.12/0.10, along +Y and −Y through the center, extending ~0.6 units beyond the sphere top and reaching the bottom of the sphere. Horizontal dashed line: black, along the screen-horizontal diameter of the equatorial ellipse, extending slightly past the ellipse on both sides. Guide lines from the electron: light blue #9FC8E0 dashed — one vertical drop from the electron straight down (−Y) to its foot point on the equatorial plane, and one from that foot point back to the center along the plane. Coulomb value for correctness: F = k e²/r² with k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C², e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C; at r = a₀ = 5.29×10⁻¹¹ m this gives F ≈ 8.25×10⁻⁸ N. Draw the arrow length proportional to 1/s² with the default (s = 1) length ≈ 0.55·R, clamped to ≤ 0.9·R so it never overshoots the proton.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the sphere silhouette with a THREE.LineLoop great circle that is re-oriented each frame to face the camera (or a MeshBasicMaterial sphere with very low opacity plus an EdgesGeometry-free outline ring) so it always reads as a clean circle during orbit. Equatorial ellipse = flat circle of radius R in the XZ plane drawn as a line loop. Dashed lines need LineDashedMaterial with computeLineDistances(). The red F arrow is best as a custom mesh (CylinderGeometry shaft + ConeGeometry head) grouped and oriented with quaternion setFromUnitVectors so it can rescale in length without distorting the head. Labels 'r' and 'F' as CSS2DRenderer/sprite labels anchored to the segment midpoint and offset a few pixels so they never overlap the arrow. Drag: raycast the pointer against an invisible sphere of radius R and snap the electron to the hit point; suppress OrbitControls while the pointer is down on the electron (set controls.enabled = false on pointerdown over the electron). Recompute the meridian arc as a QuadraticBezier/spherical interpolation between the north pole and the electron each drag frame. Slider should scale the whole shell, the electron radius position, the guide lines and the arrow together in one update function. Render order: dashed guides first, then sphere outline, then r segment, then arrow, then charges on top with depthTest disabled for the proton/electron discs so they stay visible through the shell.
